about: Skiringssal (Kaupang in Tjolling, Vestfold), 793 to 960 and the grass afterwards. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/skiringssal.md and the spine (cast.ohthere, cast.asulf, cast.thorleif, cast.tidwine, cast.crew.ravn; threads holy_island, swords_north, godfreds_market, riddle_road). No person is recorded at this market by name except Ohthere, who sailed to it: everyone else here is invented and marked so. A draft for the user to overwrite. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: In 793 there is no town here: a chieftain's hall on a height, a thing heath, a holy lake, and below them a sheltered bay behind an island where boats are drawn up and a few tents stand in summer. About 800 a market is laid out along the shore in fenced plots, most likely at a Danish king's bidding, and for four generations it is the one town of the North Way. A merchant comes for whetstones, soapstone pots, iron and the far north's furs, tooth and hide rope, and brings wine, glass, pots, grain and blades; silver is weighed here, never counted.
ports.seasons: The market is full from the end of May to the end of July; the ships of the far north come after midsummer, a month along the land. Iron and hones come down from the valleys on the last snow. The tide is slight (?), the winter bay may freeze (?), and outside the summer weeks a stranger finds a few households, a forge and an ale bench.

history.text: The oldest graves are laid on the rock by the harbour (Bikjholberget). The hall on the height at Huseby is built about this time.
history.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal (after Skre 2007); English Wikipedia, Skiringssal

history.text: A market is founded on the shore below the hall. The first buildings stand between 800 and 810, on plots laid out with fixed lanes. Who ordered it is not recorded; Dagfinn Skre holds that a Danish king did.
history.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal; snl.no/Kaupang (Stylegar 2025); the founder (?)

history.text: Posts are felled for the shore works: the oldest tree-ring date in the town.
Godfred, king of the Danes, moves the merchants of Reric to Sliesthorp, the next market south, five days' sail away.

This year the kings of the Danes, Harald and Reginfrid, went with a host to Westarfolda, the furthest part of their realm to the north-west, because its princes and people would not obey them. It is the first time Vestfold is written down.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 813 (own words after the entry, by way of English Wikipedia, Harald Klak); chronicle_793.json 813-summer-vestfold-813

history.text: While the two kings were away in the north, the sons of Godfred came back from the Svear, and before winter drove both kings out of the Danish kingdom.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 813 (from memory, not opened today) (?)

history.text: A great lady is laid in a ship under a mound further up the Vestfold coast (Oseberg), with her household goods about her.
Men of Vestfold storm Nantes on Saint John's day. What they bring home is on the market here in the autumn.
history.source: Annals of Angouleme 843 ('Westfaldingi'), by way of Design/content/realms/norway.md (?)

history.text: The latest house floors that survive the plough are of about this time. A Frisian trading household lives in one of the plots.
history.source: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal; D. Skre, From Dorestad to Kaupang (2010), not opened (?)

history.text: Ohthere of Halogaland tells King Alfred of the port called Sciringes heal: a month's sail south of his home, and five days from there to Hedeby.
history.source: The Old English Orosius (texts_793.json ohthere; J. Bosworth 1859); chronicle_793.json 890-ohthere-wulfstan

history.text: The hall at Huseby goes out of use.
The town is given up, whether for the shoaling bay or the ebb of Danish power is argued. Some trade goes on for a generation.
history.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal (Blindheim; Skre)

history.text: The last trade at Skiringssal. After this the shore is a farm's pasture.
history.source: ports_793.json; story/ages_793.json; Norwegian Wikipedia gives 'about 950 to 970' (?)

history.text: A cargo ship of oak with pine top strakes, twenty or more metres long, is built; she sinks in the next inlet east with whetstones of Eidsborg aboard, in sight of the dead town.

eras.text: A landing, not a town. The hall on the height, smoke from four or five farms, boats on the grass, and in the summer weeks a row of tents where men of the Vik, a few Danes and now and then a Frisian lay goods on cloths. The chief takes a gift and gives his protection. Nothing is built to last.

The shore is pegged out in plots with lanes between, posts are driven for a jetty, and the first small houses go up with their doors to the sea. Casters and bead-makers come from the Danish markets. People say the king of the Danes wished it; the chief says he did.

The summer of the Danish host. Two kings and their ships lie in the fjord to make Vestfold's chiefs obey; the market is shut, cattle are driven inland, and a merchant's hull is something an army can use.

The town at its height: four to six hundred people the year round, six wells, forges, moulds drying, pots from the Rhine in every house. The Danish kings are over the Vik in name. In the 830s a Frisian household settles; in 843 church silver from the Loire is sold between the booths.

The Danish kingship breaks and Vestfold is its own master. Barter gives way to weighed silver: cut dirhams, pennies, rings, and lead weights in every purse. Men of the far north come each summer with tooth, rope and furs; about 890 one of them is Ohthere.

The hall on the height stands empty and the bay grows shallow. Two houses fewer each summer. The young men are in England, Ireland and the islands. The whetstones still come down, and the mounds on the north road are still added to.
A summer market on old house floors. Grass in the lanes, the jetties rotting, a few tents and a lawman who still tries the weights. The ships that come are small and come for hones.

Pasture. The whetstones go out through other inlets, and in 998 a ship full of them is lost in the next bay. A big house stands at Huseby again in the eleventh century. Nobody on the coast can say for certain where the market was.

sites.name: The strand under the rock
sites.see: A curve of grey shingle and mud in a sheltered arm of the fjord, the long island closing the bay to seaward so the water lies flat. A dozen clinker boats are drawn up on rollers, one on her side with a man caulking her; on a slip of logs a new hull stands in her ribs. Behind, the bare rock of the graves, and high over everything the long roof of the hall. Tar smoke, weed, wood shavings, an adze knocking.
sites.see_early: In 793 this is all there is: boats on the grass, a tar pit, and tents in summer.
sites.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal (Kaupangkilen behind Lamoya; the shore 3.5 m higher than today). That small craft were drawn up, and that ships were built here, is likely and not shown (?)

sites.name: The two jetties
sites.see: Two timber jetties run out over the mud on oak posts still pale from the axe, with stone-laid paths leading down to them between the plots. A broad cargo ship from the north lies at the outer one, her yard lowered, coils of dark rope and bundled furs on the planks beside her. Porters go by bent under soapstone pots packed in moss. Gulls, the knock of hulls on posts, a smell of wet hide.
sites.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal: two timber jetties with paths; the 'stone jetties' are now read as stone-laid paths over the mud. The post date of 803: chronicle_793.json. No toll is recorded: the landing gift is ours (?)

sites.name: The booths
sites.see: A lane of trodden earth along the shore between wattle fences, each plot with a small house whose gable door faces the water and a booth of poles and sailcloth in front. On the cloths: bundles of grey hones tied in twenties, soapstone bowls, iron bars, strings of beads, a Rhineland jug with tin foil on it. A man kneels with a folding scale no bigger than his hand. Many tongues, a dog fight, fish smoke, the sweet reek of a tanning pit.
sites.see_early: Before 800 there are no fences or houses: tents on the grass above the strand for the summer weeks, and the same goods on the same cloths.
sites.source: snl.no/Kaupang (regular plots and lanes, lived in the year round; scales, weights, dirhams and deniers; pottery from the Rhineland, Frisia and the Slav shore); Norwegian Wikipedia (houses with the gable door to the sea; six wells). A summer gathering before 800 is the game's, for the spine's hook (?)

sites.name: Thordis's bench
sites.see: A low house with an earth floor and a long hearth down the middle, benches along both walls, a soapstone pot the size of a shield hanging over the fire. A broad woman fills horn cups from a tub without looking at them and looks at everybody else. Through the gable door, the bay and the boats. Smoke in the roof, malt, wet wool, dice rattling in a cup, somebody halfway through a story.
sites.source: invented; the house is the dig's kind (two pairs of roof posts, earth floor, hearth in the middle, gable door to the sea: Norwegian Wikipedia)

sites.name: Vemund's forge
sites.see: An open-sided shed set back from the houses for fear of fire: a stone hearth, a bellows of two goatskins worked by a boy, an anvil block sunk in the floor. A thick-armed man holds a sword blade to the light by its bare tang; on the wall hang hilts without blades, of bronze and of walrus tooth. Charcoal, hot iron, the hiss of the quenching trough.
sites.source: the spine's hook for swords_north (a smith who fits northern hilts to Frankish blades); a smithy at Kaupang is likely and unchecked (dossier 2) (?)

sites.name: The casters' and bead-makers' plots
sites.see: Three plots side by side where the ground is black with charcoal. A woman turns a rod of blue glass in a small clay furnace and winds a bead off it with an iron pin; next door a man breaks a clay mould from a brooch still too hot to hold. Crucibles the size of an egg, bars of brass and lead, a child sorting broken glass by colour. A pedlar has lumps of amber and a small knife.
sites.source: Norwegian Wikipedia and snl.no/Kaupang: bronze casting (crucibles, brass and lead bars, clay moulds), a jeweller's work, lead casting, glass-bead making, bone and antler work. Amber working (?)

sites.name: The shining hall at Huseby
sites.see: A hall as long as three ships on a raised platform on the height, its walls bowed like a hull, its ends narrowed, the shingles catching the low sun. From its door a man sees every boat in the bay and the whole market under him. Inside, a fire the length of the floor, carved posts, benches for sixty, the high seat on the north wall. Roast pork, pine smoke, hounds, a voice saying a poem.
sites.source: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal; snl.no/Skiringssal; Norwegian Wikipedia: dug 2000-01, 32 to 35 m by 9 to 11.5 m, on a platform over a levelled mound of the 3rd or 4th century, built mid or late 8th century, out of use about 900, looking down on the harbour. 'The shining hall' is Kare Hoel's reading of the name (1986). The furnishing is ours

sites.name: Thjodalyng, the people's heath
sites.see: A wide heath of ling and juniper a short walk north of the hall, with a ring of low stones and one standing stone grey with lichen. On a thing day a hundred men sit on the ground in their cloaks, spears stuck upright behind them, and one man stands and says the law from memory. No building at all. Wind, larks, a horse stamping, long silences between the speeches.
sites.source: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal: Thjodalyng, 'the people's heath', now Tjolling; things were still held there in 1557. No church stands on it before about 1150. The stones and the trying of weights are ours; nothing of the law's content survives (?)

sites.name: The holy lake
sites.see: A long still lake among alders, north of the heath, dark as a whetstone and without a boat on it. On a flat rock at the water's edge lie small things: a bead, a bent knife, a clipping of silver, a bowl of butter gone to the flies. An old woman with a staff sits a little way off and watches who comes. Reed warblers, midges, the smell of bog.
sites.source: English Wikipedia, Skiringssal (Brink): a lake north of Tjolling, about 1.1 km by 500 m then, ringed by place-names of worship. Which gods were honoured, and how, no source says: the offerings are ours (?)

sites.name: The rock of the boats
sites.see: A hump of bare rock and thin turf at the harbour's edge with nothing on it to mark a grave, so a stranger walks over the dead without knowing. Here and there the turf has sunk in the long shape of a boat. A woman is laying a new one out: a small boat in a cut trench, a shield, a pair of bronze brooches on a folded cloak. Below, the market goes on.
sites.source: Norwegian Wikipedia, Kaupangen i Skiringssal: Bikjholberget, 74 graves dug 1950-57, about 760 to 940, unmarked, many in boats, with weapon sets, swords and bronze brooches, three of them rich women

sites.name: The barrows on the north road
sites.see: The road from the shore to the hall runs between barrows, more than a hundred, green and round, the newest still raw earth with ash in it. Sheep graze over them. A man walking up to the hall with a gift walks the whole length of the chief's dead first, and is meant to. Evening light makes them cast long shadows across the track.
sites.source: Norwegian and English Wikipedia: Nordre Kaupang, 115 mounds recorded by Nicolaysen in 1867, mostly cremations, many of the 10th century. Ynglingatal lays King Halfdan Whiteleg in a mound at Skiringssal: a poem, not a fact (English Wikipedia, Halfdan Hvitbeinn)

sites.name: The Frisian's house
sites.see: One plot kept differently: the fence mended, a bench outside the door, Rhineland jugs on a shelf and a quern of dark southern lava by the hearth. A short man in a cloak too short for the weather counts cloth bolts against a tally stick while his wife salts butter. A small wooden cross hangs inside, where it cannot be seen from the lane. Wine, wax, and somebody singing a psalm badly.
sites.source: One house at Kaupang is read as a Frisian trading household of the 9th century (peoples/norse.md, citing Skre 2010; not opened) (?). The people and the cross are ours: no church, priest or mission is recorded here

people.name: Asgrim
people.trait: Lord of the hall on the height: courteous, slow, and never asks one question where three will do.
people.want: A market under his own hand on his own shore, before a king of the Danes plants one there.
people.fear: To end as a Danish king's steward in his fathers' hall.
people.voice: Unhurried and exact. Praises a thing a little less than it deserves and means it as praise.
people.looks: About forty-five, tall and spare, grey in a fair beard, a red cloak pinned at the shoulder with a ring pin of silver, a gold-bound horn in his hand, two grey hounds at his knee.
knows: who may trade on his shore and under whose protection
what the Danish kings want of the Vik, a season before the market hears it
the valleys the iron and the hones come down, and who brings them
which ship's chiefs of the west coast are in the fjord, and what they have to sell

ties.note: his father's sister; he asks her before any crossing and any feast
the smith is his man and forges on his land
Bard steered his ship when both were young
in name; he sends a gift each year and hopes it is taken for obedience
a west-coast ship's chief who sells on his strand and gives small gifts
the same man, at home on the Karmsund
the steward of the Danes' hall takes his yearly gift and weighs it in front of him
in the summer of the Danish host it is the woman with the keys on the Karmsund who is asked to keep what he values (the chain saga_danes_norway) (?)

lines.greet: A Frisian, in a boat that size. Sit. A man who comes so far in so little has sense or has none, and I like to know which.
lines.greet_again: You came back, and the boat is no bigger. Good. Men who grow fast leave fast.
rumour: The king of the Danes wants a market on my shore. He has not asked me. He has asked men who will tell me.
A ship's chief from the west sold strange goods here at summer's end. Gilt things with holes in them. The women bought and the men laughed.
They cut hones in the high valleys and sledge them down on the last snow. Half the blades of the south will be sharpened on my stone.
lines.gift: I take no toll. I take a gift, and then you are my guest, and who robs my guest has robbed me. It comes cheaper than a toll.
lines.kings: Two kings of the Danes are coming to ask whether I am theirs. Two kings, for one answer. It is a great honour and I could do without it.
lines.saying: A guest should bring news or go hungry. You may do both; many have.
lines.farewell: Go with the land wind. Tell them in the south there is a shore here where a man's goods stay his own.

people.source: invented. The Frankish annals for 813 speak of the 'princes' of Westarfolda who would not obey the Danish kings, and name none: he stands for one of them. The hall is real (Huseby)

people.name: Thordis
people.trait: Brews for the strand and forgets nothing: a face, a debt, who sat beside whom and who left first.
people.want: A house with a door on the shore when the plots are given out, and her daughter to keep it after her.
people.fear: A bad brew in market week; a brawl with a king's man in it.
people.voice: Talks while she pours and never spills. Tells you what you owe before she tells you the news.
people.looks: About thirty in 793, broad, strong forearms, brown hair under a linen cloth, a grey dress with two plain bronze brooches and a string of blue beads between, a ladle in her belt like a weapon.
knows: everyone who has drunk on the strand these ten summers, and what they sold
who bought the three English boys in the autumn of 793, and where he took them
that the crew kept a fourth boy, who could count, and that the Dane came back for him three summers on
which skippers are hiring, and which crews are leaving them
the price of malt, and who will have none by harvest

ties.note: her brother; she keeps his place on the bench and his debts off the tally
he mends her pot chains; she does not count his cups
Jorunn taught her the brewing herbs and what not to put in
she served him and will not again: he sold children across her bench
the same man, at home on the Schlei
the boy who counted her cups; she fed him twice and has wondered since
he drank at her mother's bench and still owes for it, she says
the chief's wife on the Karmsund takes her bead strings and pays in down; they have never met, and know each other by what each will not buy

lines.greet: You are the Frisian with the small boat. Bard said one would come. A jug is a sliver of silver, and the first is not counted.
lines.greet_again: Your place is the end of the bench by the door. I kept a drunk Dane out of it this morning. You may thank me.
rumour: A Dane bought three English boys on this strand, the autumn after the raid west. A fourth the crew kept: he counted my cups without being asked. He was right, too.
The gilt things on the dealer's cloth came off a god's house over the sea. The women wear them. I would not; somebody is missing them.
Vemund has a blade from the Rhine with a pattern like a snake's back. He keeps it nearer than his wife. She says it is quieter.
lines.boys: I never had his name. Small, cropped, held a stick like something precious. The crew kept him for the tally and took him home to the Karmsund. The Dane who had the other three is Asulf, at the Heaths. Do not drink with him.
lines.boys_later: The counting boy came through again three summers on, in the Dane's boat, bound east. He knew my cups. He did not know me.
lines.heir: Your father sat there. He paid on the second asking, every time. You have his boat. I hope you have not his habit.
lines.saying: Praise ale when it is drunk. Ale that is owed is another matter.
lines.farewell: Come before the leaves turn or not till the cuckoo. In between I brew for myself.

people.source: invented. The saying turns Havamal 81 (Bellows 1923). What she knows of the boys is the spine's hook for holy_island

people.name: Vemund
people.trait: A hilt smith who trusts no iron he has not bent over his own knee, and no man who will not let him.
people.want: Frankish blades bare of hilts, a steady hand to bring them, and his mark known from the Vik to the Karmsund.
people.fear: A sword of his breaking in a man's hand, with his name on the grip.
people.voice: Short and rude until the iron is good; then shorter, and nearly polite.
people.looks: Late twenties in 793, not tall, very wide, burn scars up both forearms, a leather apron, singed fair hair tied back with a thong, a small hammer through his belt.
knows: what a Frankish blade fetches with a northern hilt on it, and from whom
which ship's chiefs are buying swords this year
good iron from bad by its ring on the anvil
how blades come past the Frankish tolls, though he says he does not ask

ties.note: forges on the chief's land and hilts the chief's swords first
drinks there; mends her chains for it
Thorleif's swords are his best trade and his worst customer
both want the same blades; Asulf can pay in people
six hilts promised before the cuckoo
learned casting from him at the Danes' summer market, and was weighed there like everybody else (?)
the wright on the Karmsund owes him for a winter's rivets, and sends excuses better made than most men's payments

lines.greet: Show me your knife. No, the edge, not the handle. Hm. Frisian iron. It will cut cheese.
lines.greet_again: You again. Have you brought iron, or only talk? I can have talk from my wife.
rumour: The Franks' king forbids his blades to leave his land. So they cost more, and come anyway, under salt. I do not ask under what.
Thorleif of the west coast wants six swords hilted before the cuckoo. He pays in walrus tooth. Good for grips, bad for bread.
A Dane called Asulf buys blades with people. I buy them with silver. Sell to me. You will sleep better, and so will I.
lines.blades: Bring me blades bare. The Frankish hilt is a clerk's hilt. I put a man's grip on it, and we share what it fetches.
lines.letters: There is a smith on the Rhine who puts his name in the iron. I cannot read it. I can read the blade.
lines.test: I bend it to my knee. If it comes back straight, I buy. If it stays bent, you have a fine pot hook.
lines.saying: Praise a weapon when it is tried. Until then it is only dear.
lines.farewell: Keep the blades dry and your mouth shut at the tolls. In that order.

people.source: invented; the spine's hook for swords_north. Blades with a maker's name inlaid (ULFBERHT) are from about 800 (goods_793.json sword_blades): the line 'letters' is for years after 800. The saying turns Havamal 81 (Bellows 1923)

people.name: Bard
people.trait: A Vik skipper who knows every skerry by the sound the swell makes on it, and passes on riddles as other men pass on colds.
people.want: His son home from the west with something to say for himself.
people.fear: Fog among the skerries; and that the boy likes Thorleif's trade better than his.
people.voice: Dry, with long pauses. Gives a sailing direction as if it were an insult, and an insult as if it were a sailing direction.
people.looks: Past forty, lean and stooped from a low boat, a white scar through one eyebrow, a sealskin hood pushed back, a sounding line coiled over his shoulder and a rune-cut stick in his belt.
knows: the way in among the skerries and the island, by day and by the sound of it in fog
five days to the Heaths, and where to lie each night
the coast north as far as the Karmsund
one of the three riddles of Aegir's daughters, and who has the other two
that he and Ravn sat on one bench at Hleidr, and what was asked there

ties.note: his sister; he drinks on her tally
steered the chief's ship when both were young
bench-fellows at Hleidr long ago; neither says how long
the same man, in the house's own boat
his son rows on Thorleif's ship and came home quiet
the ferryman on the Schlei has the third riddle; they sat on the same bench
the skald has the second riddle and sells what Bard gives away
the watchman at the Danes' landing; Bard lies there windbound most autumns with a load of hones
the blind reciter at Hleidr, off whose bench the riddles come (?)
the old steersman on the Karmsund says no man of the Vik can find his sound; Bard has found it twenty times and says so each time
brings the old woman fish and never asks an omen
the poet on the Karmsund forgives him for giving riddles away, because he brings news

lines.greet: You came in between the wrong two skerries and lived. Either you are lucky or Ravn is aboard. Ah. Ravn is aboard.
lines.greet_again: The small boat. I knew the sail before the hull. Next time keep the bare rock to steerboard until the hall roof opens.
rumour: Five days to the Heaths with a fair wind. Three with open sea to steerboard, two among the Danes' islands. Fewer, if you do not sleep.
The men of the far north come after midsummer, a month along the land. They sell rope cut from a sea beast. I have hung an anchor on it.
My son went west with Thorleif and came back with a silver cup and nothing to say. I liked him better talkative.
lines.riddle: Ravn answers in riddles. I had one off the same bench. Who are the maids that go weeping to the joy of their father? Take your time. They do.
lines.ravn: Ask Ravn what he was asked at Hleidr. No. Do not. Ask him when you have known him ten winters.
lines.saying: Short are the yards of a ship, and autumn nights are uneasy. My father said it. His father drowned saying it.
lines.farewell: Go out on the land wind before sunrise. By noon the sea wind sets you back on the skerries, and I have other work.

people.source: invented: the 'Vestfold skipper' of riddles_793.json r-gest-21 and of the spine's hook for riddle_road. The riddle's words are Gestumblindi's, from the saga of King Heidrek (Vigfusson and Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, 1883; texts_793.json t-gest-21). The saying turns Havamal 74 (Bellows 1923). No source opened names a channel or a mark here: the skerries are the modern coast carried back (?)

people.name: Jorunn
people.trait: The woman with the staff, who sits by the lake, washes the dead for the rock, and says what she sees as flatly as a price.
people.want: To be laid on the rock sitting up in the stern of a good boat, with her staff across her knees.
people.fear: A dry summer that shows what lies on the lake bed; a child she delivered signed with the Christians' cross.
people.voice: Flat, a little bored. Never says 'perhaps'. Charges for everything, and tells you so first.
people.looks: Nearly sixty in 793, small and straight, white hair in one plait, a dark blue cloak with catskin at the neck (?), an iron staff with a knob of bronze, a pouch at her belt that rattles.
knows: what is given at the lake before a crossing, and what is asked for
who lies in which grave on the rock, though nothing marks them
herbs for fever, for wounds and for the brew
the chief's mind, a day before he knows it

ties.note: his father's sister; he does not cross water without asking her
taught her the brewing herbs
he brings her fish and never asks an omen, which she respects
the one man off a southern boat who greets the lake before he greets her
there is another with a staff on the Karmsund; each says the other guesses (?)

lines.greet: A Christian. I can smell the wax. Stand where you are. The lake does not mind you, and neither do I, at that distance.
lines.greet_again: You again, and still alive. Then what I told you was true, or you did not listen. Either way you owe me.
rumour: They burn their dead on the north road and boat them on the rock. Ask me which is better and I will ask who is paying.
Men throw silver in the lake before a sea crossing. In a dry summer I could tell you how much. I do not go and look.
The chief greets his fathers' mounds going out and coming in. They have not answered yet. He is a patient man.
lines.omen: You want to know if the crossing is good. Look at the gulls, then at your ropes. If both are sound, pay me anyway. I have told you true.
lines.staff: The staff is not for leaning on. When I die they will sit me in a boat's stern with it. I have chosen the boat. He does not know.
lines.saying: Praise the day at evening. I have washed too many who praised it at noon.
lines.farewell: Go. Something looks on you with favour. I would not lean on it.

people.source: invented, after a boat grave on Bikjholberget with a man, a woman and a second woman seated at the stern with a staff, read as a seeress (dossier 7; not checked on a page opened) (?). The catskin is from a saga's seeress, three hundred years later (?). The saying turns Havamal 81 (Bellows 1923)

people.name: Folkmar
people.trait: A Frisian of Dorestad who moved his house north after the first burning, reasoning that nobody robs his own market.
people.want: News from the Rhine, in Frisian; a priest, once, before he dies.
people.fear: That his children will grow up weighing silver and knowing no prayer; that the wine will stop coming.
people.voice: Quick and dry, glad of his own tongue. Complains as a courtesy.
people.looks: About thirty-five in 835, short, clean-shaven chin and a long moustache, a striped cloak too short for the north, a folding scale in a tin case at his belt, a tally stick behind his ear.
knows: what wine, cloth and Rhineland pots fetch here, and in which week
how the Northmen weigh, nick and cut silver, and how they cheat at it
who in the fjord was at Dorestad or on the Loire, and what they brought back
where a Christian may lodge and store goods over a winter

ties.note: pays Rorik's due when his wine comes down through Dorestad after 850
the Dane at Dorestad's toll passes his casks and sends him news
the same man, at the toll
trades under the Danish king's peace, such as it is, until 854
from 857 a Frisian priest at Ripa is the nearest Mass, and the nearest man to confess to in his own tongue
sends the bishop word of the Vik by any ship, and asks in return only when a priest might come; none has

lines.greet: God keep you. Frisian? From where? Speak slowly, I want every word. Nobody here can say 'butter' properly.
lines.greet_again: Come in, mind the hearth. I have Rhine wine in a jug with tin on it, and nobody to drink it with who knows what it is.
rumour: Dorestad has burned again, I hear. I left after the first time. Here I live among the men who do it, and they pay on the day.
The Northmen weigh everything now. Bring coin and they cut it like cheese. Bring a scale of your own, or bring a friend.
Men of this fjord were on the Loire. There is an altar cup in the market. I bought it. I do not yet know what I shall do.
lines.mass: No priest north of the Danes' wall. On Sundays I say what I remember and my wife corrects me. If you know the Creed whole, stay to supper.
lines.store: Leave your wine with me over winter. I charge a twentieth and I do not drink it. I say so because my neighbours offer cheaper.
lines.saying: A Frisian abroad needs three things: a scale, a short cloak, and somebody to complain to.
lines.farewell: Greet the Rhine for me. Tell it I am well and the ale here is thin.

people.source: invented, for the Frisian trading household read from one house at Kaupang (Skre 2010, by way of peoples/norse.md) (?). Dorestad was raided in 834, 835, 836 and 837 (Annales Bertiniani); Nantes fell to men of Vestfold in 843: the third rumour is for years after 843. The short cloak is Notker's joke on the Frisians (Gesta Karoli i.34, Grant 1907)

people.name: Ohthere
people.trait: Rich by northern reckoning, six hundred tame deer and the tribute of the Finnas, and a careful witness: says what he saw himself and marks what he was only told.
people.want: A market in the south for walrus tooth and hide rope; to know how far north the land runs.
people.fear: Not recorded. (Ours: the Cwenas, who carry their boats over the mountains to raid.)
people.voice: Understated. Measures everything in days' sail and says which hand the land was on.
people.looks: About fifty, tall, weather-dark, a walrus-ivory comb and knife handle, a cloak of fine marten, a coil of hide rope and a pair of tusks carried behind him as a gift for a king.
knows: the coast from Halogaland to here: a month, anchoring at night, the land always on one hand
what the Finnas pay him, by each man's birth
how the horse-whale is hunted and what his tooth and hide are good for
five days from here to the Heaths, and what lies on each hand

ties.note: the same person
their two accounts were written down together for the same king
the same man, met at the Heaths
the lawman witnesses his sales each summer and is paid in rope
the king's man on the Karmsund takes a share of every northern cargo that passes
a woman of Skane took hide rope of him at the Heaths on a promise of cloth; he has marked that she was only told to, not seen to, weave it

lines.greet: You are from the south. Then tell me one thing you saw yourself. I have had my fill of what men were told.
lines.greet_again: The southerner. I counted the days since you left: more than a month, less than two. So you did not go far, or you came back fast.
rumour: From my home a man could not sail here in a month, anchoring at night, with fair wind each day. I had fair wind most days. I say most.
North of me there is waste. I went to look. Three days, then three more, and the land bent east. I say what I saw.
The Finnas pay in marten, deer, bear, feathers and rope. The Cwenas pay nothing, and carry boats over the mountains to take what they like.
lines.wealth: Six hundred deer, unsold, and twenty cattle. At home I am among the first men. Here a bead-maker asked if I had come to sell my coat.
lines.south: Five days from here to the Heaths. Further I have not been. They say a king in the west asks questions and has the answers written.
lines.saying: Keep the land on one hand all day and at evening you know where you are. Men who cut corners can tell you less.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you see a horse-whale's tooth carved in the south, look at it well. I shall ask.

people.source: The Old English Orosius (texts_793.json ohthere; J. Bosworth 1859): the month's sail, the six hundred deer, the twenty cattle, the Finnas' tribute, the Cwenas, the five days to Hedeby. The spine's cast.ohthere, with the same facts. His birth year and all his spoken words here are ours (?); the chain walrus_ivory carries his story

people.name: Hallmund
people.trait: Says the law on the heath and tries the weights at the stone; has watched the town get smaller every summer of his life and kept its rules the same size.
people.want: That whatever is done here, down to the last bargain, is done before witnesses.
people.fear: To be the man who says the law to an empty heath.
people.voice: Formal, in threes, like a man reciting. Dry when he stops reciting.
people.looks: A long thin man, thirty in 885 and white-haired by 920, a plain undyed cloak, a set of lead weights in a leather bag round his neck, a hazel rod in his hand.
knows: the law of sale, witness and weight as it is said at Thjodalyng
who has left for England, Ireland or the islands, and who keeps their plot
where the bay has shoaled and which jetty still takes a laden ship
who brings the hones down, and what they will take for the whole sledge

ties.note: witnesses the northerner's sales and likes a man who says only what he saw
her daughter's son; he learned to count on her tally sticks
the Dublin king's poet has kin in the Vik and sends word by the ships each summer (?)
the king's men of the west say the law runs from the king; he says it runs from the heath

lines.greet: A stranger with goods. Then hear it once: weights are tried at the stone, quarrels wait for the thing, and knives stay in belts on the heath.
lines.greet_again: You know the law here by now. There is less of it than there was, and fewer to break it.
rumour: The bay is shallower than when I was a boy. I wade as a man where my father moored. The young say I have grown. I have not.
The hall on the height stands empty. The roof went in my time. People still look up at it before they name a price.
Every summer two houses fewer. The men are in England with land of their own, or in Ireland with somebody else's.
lines.law: A sale is good with two witnesses and a handshake. A sale at night is no sale. If you bought at night, you found it.
lines.last: You may be the last keel I see here. I will witness your bargain all the same. Somebody should remember it was done properly.
lines.saying: With law the land is built. Without it you get a market.
lines.farewell: Go in peace. If you owe anyone here, pay before the wind turns. The thing is a long way to come back to.

people.source: invented. Things were held at Thjodalyng (English Wikipedia, Skiringssal); nothing of the law's content survives from these years, so his rules are ours (?). The saying turns 'with law shall the land be built', a proverb written down in the 13th century (Frostathing law; LATER)

stories.title: The one who could count
stories.summary: In the autumn of 793 a west-coast ship's chief sold his summer's takings on this strand: church things nobody had a use for, and three English boys. A fourth, who could count, the crew kept for three summers more. The gilt lies on a dealer's cloth, and the ale-wife remembers the boy who counted her cups, and the Dane who took the others south and came back for him.
stories.picture: The strand at dusk in autumn: a broad woman with a ladle in a doorway, looking after three small cropped boys being walked down to a ship by a stout man with a hazel switch; in the foreground a cloth with a gilt strip, a cup and a little house-shaped box.

beats.text: Bishop Higbald counts off the boys' names and what the house can pay for each. One of them, Tidwine, wrote a fair hand at twelve. (Sets lf_knows_boys.)

Between the hones and the soapstone a dealer has church things laid out as curios: a little box shaped like a house, a cup, a strip of gilt with rivet holes. The women buy the knotwork. The men ask what it weighs.

Thordis tells it while she pours: three English boys on the strand the autumn after the raid, sold by Thorleif's men to a Dane called Asulf, who took them south to Sliesthorp. A fourth, who counted her cups unasked, the crew kept for the tally and took home to the Karmsund. (Sets lf_trail_north.)
In a later summer the big red-fair chief is on the strand again with a box of sewn calfskins he could not sell, the gold broken off the lid. He will take swords or silver for it, not prayers.

Asulf remembers every sale. The three of 793 went east with a Svea at summer's end. The boy who could count came through his pen three summers later, went to the same Svea, who wanted a tally-keeper, and fetched more than the other three together.
In Holmfast's booth a servant in northern dress notches a tally and holds the stick like a pen. He answers to no English name until he hears his own. (Sets lf_boy_found.)
Beside the strip of gilt lie a little house-shaped box, a cup, and painted calfskins sold as patterns. The dealer tipped the bones out of the box. Nobody buys bones.
On the heath above Thorleif's hall two English boys herd swine. One of them holds his stick like a pen and writes in the mud. (Sets lf_boy_found.)

endings.how: Asked Thordis, carried her word south to Asulf and east to Birka, and found the boy.
endings.text: Tidwine is found, a man or nearly, tallying furs for a Svea. Whether he sails home is his to say and the thread's to tell. Thordis asks each summer after and is told the truth.
endings.reward: The flag lf_trail_north, and through it lf_boy_found; Thordis a fast friend for this house and its heirs; the bishop's thanks when word reaches the island.

endings.how: Bought the house-shaped box, the cup and the gilt strip off the dealer's cloth and carried them back to the island.
endings.text: The box held a saint's bones once and holds them again. The brethren pay in wax and in prayers said by name, and a Northumbrian reeve is easier with a man the bishop speaks for.
endings.reward: About forty pennies' weight laid out, some two hundred pennies' worth of wax and wine back; a good deed toward the church; standing in Northumbria.

endings.how: Bought the gilt for what it weighed and sold it for what it weighed.
endings.text: It is silver and bronze like any other. Thordis sees it go into your scale and fills your cup a little less full after that, for a summer.
endings.reward: A few pennies' gain; Thordis cool for a season; nothing learned.

stories.reward: The trail of the boys of Lindisfarne (lf_trail_north), or the island's goods carried home, and in either case somebody on this strand who remembers what you did about it.

stories.title: A man's grip
stories.summary: The best blades in the north are Frankish and the king's law says they stay in Francia. Vemund wants them bare of hilts, fits grips of bronze and walrus tooth, and sells them to the ship's chiefs of the west coast for three times what they cost on the Rhine. He needs one man who can bring them past the tolls.
stories.picture: A forge shed at night: a wide scarred smith bending a bright blade across his knee, a Frisian watching with his hand half raised to stop him, a row of hilts without blades hanging on the wall behind.

beats.text: Vemund looks at your knife, then shows you a blade from the Rhine with his own hilt on it. He wants more like it, without the hilts, and will share what they fetch.
A blade without its hilt is cheaper and lies flat under a cargo. The smith who sells it does not ask where it is going and would rather not be told.

Since the emperor's order of 805 no arms go out of the realm. The tollman's men probe the salt with rods. Declared, the blades are forfeit; hidden and found, so is the boat. (Hidden and not found sets sw_ran_blades.)
Vemund bends each blade to his knee, keeps those that come back straight, and names his buyer: Thorleif of the Karmsund, who pays a walrus tusk for a hilted sword. (Sets sw_buyer_known.)
Thorleif draws one of Vemund's swords half out and asks who carried it north. He laughs before he says anything else, which with him can mean either thing.

endings.how: Brought bare blades north in more than one summer and let Vemund hilt and sell them.
endings.text: Vemund's mark and your cargo become one trade. He tells nobody your name and everybody your price. In the west the king's men have a description of a small Frisian boat.
endings.reward: A standing order: each blade brought to Vemund pays about three times its Rhine price, a good voyage's worth on every run; Vemund fits and mends this house's own arms and tools at cost; the risk of sw_marked at every Frankish toll.

endings.how: Ran one cargo, took the silver and did not come back with another.
endings.text: Vemund says it was good iron and does not ask twice. A year on, a Dane on the strand wears one of the swords, and you know the hilt.
endings.reward: One large payment in weighed silver, in the range of a good voyage twice over; the flag sw_buyer_known; no more is asked.

endings.how: Told Vemund no, and told him why.
endings.text: He shrugs, and sells you an axe that will outlast the boat. He thinks more of a man who says no at once than of one who says yes and is searched.
endings.reward: Nothing lost. Tools and rivets at the smith's own price here; a clean name at the tolls.

stories.reward: A buyer in the north known by name (sw_buyer_known) and a smith who works for this house, or a clean name and good tools: the law's risk decides which.

stories.title: Two kings for one answer
stories.summary: The king of the Danes wants a market on the chief's shore and gets one; five years after Godfred moves Reric's merchants to Sliesthorp, his successors Harald and Reginfrid bring a host to make Vestfold obey. Asgrim has a daughter, a chest and a hall to lose, and a merchant's boat lies under it when the ships come in.
stories.picture: The bay in high summer, full of long ships with their shields along the rails; on the height the hall with its doors shut; on the strand a tall grey-bearded man in a red cloak walking down alone to meet two kings.

beats.text: Posts are being driven on the shore and plots pegged out. Asgrim says it is his market. His steward says the Danish king's man chose where the lanes run. A plot may be had now by anyone the chief calls guest.
Merchants of Reric, set down here by King Godfred's ships, sell from tents inside the new wall. They say the king asks no one where a market should be.

Word comes up the coast: Harald and Reginfrid are gathering ships to make the Vik obey. Asgrim asks whether a small boat nobody would look at twice could carry his daughter and one chest to the Karmsund.
The Danish host lies in the fjord. The market is shut, cattle are gone inland, and the kings' men pay well for grain, ale and any hull that can carry. Asgrim walks down to them alone.

The oaths sworn on the heath last summer were sworn to two kings who by winter had no kingdom: Godfred's sons came home from the Svear and drove them out. Asgrim tells it without smiling, and it takes him some effort.

endings.how: Carried Asgrim's daughter and his chest round to the Karmsund before the ships came, and brought both back in 814.
endings.text: The hall stands, the chief has sworn, and what he valued was never where the kings could count it. He seats you above his steward and tells the story as if the plan were his.
endings.reward: Asgrim's guest-right for this house and its heirs: no landing gift, his protection in the Vik, and a plot on the shore for nothing; a friend at Ogvaldsnes who saw you keep a trust.

endings.how: Stayed through the summer of 813 and sold grain, ale and carriage to the Danish host.
endings.text: The kings' men pay in good silver and pay twice the market. By winter the kings are gone from Denmark and their favour is worth nothing. The Vik remembers who fed them.
endings.reward: Several hundred pennies in weighed silver in one summer; Asgrim and Thordis cool for years; no standing with the Danes that outlasts the autumn.

endings.how: Heard the news in the south and kept clear of the Vik all that year.
endings.text: The first ship into the bay in 814 finds a market that has had no wine, salt or glass for a year and a half, and a strand full of unsold hones.
endings.reward: A first cargo at shortage prices, both ways; nothing risked and nobody's thanks.

stories.reward: The chief's guest-right, a summer's hard silver, or the first cargo after a war: what the house did while two kings asked one question.

stories.title: Aegir's daughters
stories.summary: Bard has a riddle off a bench at Hleidr and gives it away to anyone who sails with Ravn. It has two sisters, one with a ferryman on the Schlei and one with a skald at Birka, and all three have the same answer. The chief on the height gives a ship to the guest who can say all three and what they share.
stories.picture: A lean skipper on an upturned boat, holding up a rune-cut stick against a grey bay where lines of white-topped waves run in past the skerries; Ravn standing a little apart, not looking at either of them.

beats.text: Ravn sets his first riddle and will not say where he learned the habit.
Bard knows the boat by Ravn in it. He gives a stick with one riddle cut on it: the maids who go weeping to the joy of their father. He says there are two more, and who has them.
The ferryman on the Schlei has the third sister: the brides that walk over the reefs. He gives it for the crossing fee and asks after Bard.
A skald sells the second for silver, as skalds do. He too sat on a bench with Ravn, long ago, in the Danes' hall. (Sets rd_setter_known.)
At the chief's fire a guest may say all three and the one answer. Ravn, if he lives, sits at the door end and looks at the roof.

endings.how: Gathered the three sticks at Skiringssal, Sliesthorp and Birka and answered them before the chief.
endings.text: The chief says a man who can find one thing in three harbours should have a ship fit to visit more. A hull of the Vik's own build is drawn down the strand for you.
endings.reward: The riddle set's reward rw_ship_vestfold: a Norse all-round ship as a chief's gift (ship class norse_allround_ship); the flag rd_setter_known.

endings.how: Answered Bard's riddle and went no further.
endings.text: Bard nods as if you had tied a decent knot. He walks you out along the rocks at low water and shows you the way in, once, without repeating himself.
endings.reward: Bard's marks: the way in among the skerries needs no pilot for this house; Bard a friend; the riddle in the chest.

endings.text: Ravn gives it, as another riddle. Bard hears of it by evening and says only that some men are carried over water and some swim.
endings.reward: The answer and a second riddle to carry; no gift from the hall; Ravn, oddly, a little warmer.

stories.reward: A ship of the Vik's build as a chief's gift, or the skipper's marks, and the knowledge that the north's riddles all pass along one old bench (rd_setter_known).

stories.title: Grass in the lanes
stories.summary: After 900 the hall is empty, the bay shoals and the households leave two by two. Hallmund still tries the weights and says the law. A merchant who keeps coming is, in the end, most of the market, and may decide what leaves with him.
stories.picture: A shore of sunken house floors and leaning fence posts under a wide pale sky, grass in the lanes, one rotten jetty; a long thin white-haired man with a hazel rod standing beside a single small boat and a stack of bundled hones.

beats.text: Hallmund says the law to forty men where his grandfather heard it said to four hundred. He asks whether Frisians still want hones, and how many a boat like yours can carry.
The inner jetty stands in mud at every state of the water. A household is loading everything it owns, loom and quern and hearth stones, for the Irish shore, and has more than its boat will hold.
Along the black pool the houses are built as at home: two pairs of posts, the hearth in the middle, the door in the gable. A man from the Vik knows your boat and asks if the lake is still there.
Three tents on old floors. The hone men have come down with one sledge load and no other buyer. Hallmund, very old, has the lead weights out all the same.

endings.how: Came for the hones every summer to the end and let Hallmund witness the last bargain.
endings.text: He hangs the bag of lead weights round your neck, since there will be nobody to try them against. The hone men agree to meet your boat in the next inlet from now on.
endings.reward: The whetstone trade of the Vik for this house after 960, bought at the source; the thing's lead weights (a true northern scale: the flag sv_scale if it is not yet held).

endings.how: Carried the household and its goods over the sea to the Irish shore.
endings.text: They build the same house on another strand and keep a place by its hearth for the boat that brought them. Their children speak two tongues and haggle in both.
endings.reward: A friend's house at Duiblinn: lodging, storage and news there for this house and its heirs; a good deed among the Northmen.

endings.how: Took the trade elsewhere when the bay grew too shallow.
endings.text: One summer nobody remarks that the Frisian boat did not come, because there is nobody to remark it.

stories.reward: The Vik's hones at their source after the market is gone, or a hearth among the Northmen of Ireland: what a house keeps of a town that is forgotten.

works.name: Posts for the outer jetty
works.what: Oak posts and planking for the second jetty, driven into the mud in the first years of the market. The men who pay for posts tie up at them.
works.needs: The chief at least easy with you, and a summer when the market is being laid out.
works.gives: A berth of your own at the jetty: loading in half the time and at any state of the water, and no waiting behind a bigger ship. Inherited while the jetty stands.
works.picture: Men up to their thighs in grey mud swinging a heavy maul onto a pale oak post, a line of posts already running out into the bay, the hall on the height behind.
works.source: Two timber jetties were dug at Kaupang; shore posts are tree-ring dated to about 803 (Norwegian Wikipedia; chronicle_793.json). That merchants paid for them is ours (?)

works.name: A plot on the shore
works.what: One of the fenced plots along the lane, with a small house of two pairs of posts, an earth floor, a hearth and a gable door to the sea. The town was laid out in such plots from the first.
works.needs: The chief's leave (or after 900 the lawman's), and two witnesses at the thing.
works.gives: A house here: lodging for nothing, a boatload stored dry, a place to winter, and a booth in the market without the stranger's gift.
works.picture: A new wattle fence round a patch of trodden earth, a small thatched house going up with its door to the bay, a Frisian and a carpenter pacing out the hearth.
works.source: snl.no/Kaupang (regular plots and fixed lanes); Norwegian Wikipedia (the houses). How a plot was held is not recorded (?)

works.name: A stone-laid path to the water
works.what: Flat stones laid in a line across the soft foreshore from the lane to the jetty, so that a loaded man does not sink to the knee.
works.needs: A plot, or a berth at the jetty.
works.gives: Porters cost less and break less: no loss in loading pots, glass or wine here. The neighbours use it too and say so.
works.picture: A line of flat grey stones running across shining mud to a jetty, a porter walking it upright with a soapstone pot on his shoulder, another beside the path sunk to his shins.
works.source: The 'stone jetties' once claimed at Kaupang are now read as stone-laid paths across the muddy shore (Norwegian Wikipedia)

works.name: A wattle-lined well
works.what: A shaft dug behind the plots and lined with woven hazel, with a lid against the hens. Six such wells were found in the town.
works.needs: A plot, or the goodwill of the ale-wife, who wants one nearer her house.
works.gives: Sweet water at your own door: provisioning here takes no time, and Thordis or her daughter thinks better of you every brewing day.
works.picture: A round shaft lined with woven hazel rods, a bucket of staves on a rope, a woman with her sleeves rolled looking down into it with approval.
works.source: Six wells and wattle-lined pits at Kaupang (Norwegian Wikipedia)

ships.note: Every farm on the fjord has one and builds its own: four or six oars, light enough for two men to drag. The dead are laid in them on the rock, so a good one is not always for sale.
ships.picture: A slim clinker rowing boat on the shingle with her oars laid inside, a farmer holding her stem and naming a price to the sky.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat; the boat graves of Bikjholberget (Norwegian Wikipedia)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The Vik's build: oak below, pine in the top strakes, a hull that sails, rows and takes the ground. The timber is at the door and the rivets are Vemund's. Also a chief's gift, for the man who answers Aegir's three daughters.
ships.picture: A ship in her ribs on a slip of logs above the strand in snow, pale new planking half way up her sides, a wright sighting along the keel with one eye shut.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship; the Klastad ship of 998, oak with pine top strakes (Norwegian Wikipedia, Klastadskipet); riddles_793.json rw_ship_vestfold. A yard at Kaupang itself is not shown (?)

sayings.text: Give praise to the day at evening, to a woman on her pyre, to a weapon which is tried, to a maid at wedlock, to ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
Too early to many a meeting I came, and some too late have I sought; the beer was all drunk, or not yet brewed; little the loathed man finds.
No great thing needs a man to give, oft little will purchase praise; with half a loaf and a half-filled cup a friend full fast I made.
He welcomes the night whose fare is enough, (short are the yards of a ship,) uneasy are autumn nights.
Thither he said that a man could not sail in a month, if he anchored at night, and every day had a fair wind.
sayings.source: Ohthere, in the Old English Orosius (J. Bosworth 1859; texts_793.json ohthere)

sayings.text: A hone is the one trader who grows thinner with every bargain.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a riddle's turn; compare Tatwine's riddle 39 on the whetstone)

sayings.text: The Dane asks whose man you are. The Frisian asks what it weighs. Up here they ask both, and then what you saw.
Ask three men what Skiring means and you will have four answers, and a fifth from the old woman, for silver.
sayings.source: invented; the name's first part still defeats the scholars (Brink, by way of English Wikipedia, Skiringssal)

sayings.text: He has been to the Heaths: now every skerry is a small one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a Northman's understatement)

easter_eggs.text: On the amber pedlar's cloth among the beads lies a little foot carved of amber, toes and all, pierced to hang at the neck. He will not say what it is for. Nobody has known since.
easter_eggs.source: An amber amulet in the shape of a foot was found at Kaupang (snl.no/Kaupang)

easter_eggs.text: In a weigher's purse, among cut silver, is one small gold coin with a ship on it (?), struck at Dorestad. He keeps it for luck and will not put it in the scale.
easter_eggs.source: A gold coin from Dorestad was found at Kaupang (English Wikipedia, Kaupang); what is on it was not checked (?)

easter_eggs.text: A monk's riddle in the chest, Tatwine's thirty-ninth, has a whetstone for its answer. Solved, it gives the freshest word on what hones fetch here: a Canterbury archbishop pointing a merchant to a heathen market.
After 841 a man home from the Irish shore says the houses at the black pool are built exactly like these, door in the gable and all. He thinks it remarkable. He built two of them.
easter_eggs.source: The house type at Kaupang is that of Norse Dublin (Norwegian Wikipedia)

easter_eggs.text: After Jorunn's death there is a new sunken boat shape on the rock. Those who helped say three lie in it: a man, a woman, and at the stern an old woman sitting up with an iron staff.
easter_eggs.source: A boat grave on Bikjholberget with a seated woman and a staff, read as a seeress (dossier 7) (?)

easter_eggs.text: The poets say a king called Halfdan Whiteleg lies in one of the mounds on the north road. Ask which, and every farm points to a different one.
easter_eggs.source: Ynglingatal, by way of English Wikipedia (Skiringssal; Halfdan Hvitbeinn): a poem, shaped later

easter_eggs.text: A house that sails past after 998 may see mast and yard standing out of the water in the next inlet east: a big ship gone down at her moorings with a full load of hones, in sight of the grass where the market was.
easter_eggs.source: The Klastad ship, built 998, sank in Klastadkilen with Eidsborg whetstones aboard (Norwegian Wikipedia, Klastadskipet)

easter_eggs.text: In the game's last years nobody on this coast can say where Skiringssal's market stood. It will be argued over until a man named Munch points at the right bay in 1850.
easter_eggs.source: snl.no/Kaupang; Norwegian Wikipedia: P. A. Munch placed it in 1850 and Charlotte Blindheim dug it from 1950

easter_eggs.text: From 860 the skald's hardest riddle, answered, names a place up the river to the north-east where a great weight of gold was put in the ground.
easter_eggs.source: riddles_793.json reward rw_hoard_hon: the Hon hoard, about 2.5 kg of gold, buried in the 860s (?), found in 1834

unlocks.what: The guest-right of the hall at Huseby
unlocks.how: End 'Two kings for one answer' by carrying the chief's daughter and chest to safety and bringing them home.
unlocks.gives: No landing gift at Skiringssal; the chief's protection in the Vik (raider cards are less likely within a day's sail); a plot for nothing; inherited while the hall stands (to 900).

unlocks.what: The way in among the skerries, by heart
unlocks.how: Answer Bard's riddle (r-gest-21), or sail in three summers running with Ravn aboard.
unlocks.gives: learn (the Skiringssal marks): no pilot is needed and nothing is doubtful in the approach, in fog or by night; inherited.

unlocks.what: A ship of the Vik's build, as a chief's gift
unlocks.how: Gather Aegir's three daughters at Skiringssal, Sliesthorp and Birka and answer them in the hall.

unlocks.what: A standing order for bare blades
unlocks.how: End 'A man's grip' as Vemund's partner.
unlocks.gives: commission sword_blades at about three times the Rhine price each summer while Vemund lives; flag sw_buyer_known; repairs and tools at cost at his forge.

unlocks.how: Come back in three different summers, pay the tally each time, and tell her the truth about the boys.
unlocks.gives: npc alewife feeling up, carried to her daughter and to the heirs of this house; rumours here are never stale and cost no silver; crew hired here are loyal.

unlocks.what: The Vik's whetstones at their source
unlocks.how: End 'Grass in the lanes' as the last keel.
unlocks.gives: Whetstones bought at the sledge price after 960, met at the next inlet though the port is closed; the lawman's lead weights (flag sv_scale).

unlocks.how: Tell him plainly what tooth fetches in the south, and bring back what you saw yourself (the chain walrus_ivory).
unlocks.gives: First refusal on walrus ivory and hide rope each summer from 886 to 896; npc merchant feeling up at the Karmsund.
